summary_new: UAL (United) hedged fuel in 2000 with an options-based program, but the Item 7A text says it is no longer entering new option contracts. The excerpts show only a 1999 year-end fuel position ($1.1 billion of crude call options, fair value $120 million) and none for 2000 year-end.

UAL had fuel hedges (crude and heating oil swaps/forwards; 26% of 2002 consumption hedged) but all were terminated by counterparties on Dec 9, 2002 after the Chapter 11 filing, leaving it completely unhedged at year-end 2002. Classified as stopped_hedging (involuntary), with 2,458 million gallons consumed in 2002.

UAL Corp's FY2003 10-K says it uses crude and heating oil forwards and options from time to time, but all fuel hedges were terminated by counterparties after its Chapter 11 filing, so none are outstanding at year-end. Gallons consumed in 2003 were 2,202 million.

UAL began hedging in Q2 2004 using heating-oil collars (purchased calls plus sold puts), with about 11% of 2005 fuel requirements hedged at year-end 2004. Fair value of the contracts was about $3 million, and 32% of Q1 2005 expected consumption was hedged.

UAL had no fuel hedges outstanding at December 31, 2005, though it had run a collar-based hedging program since Q2 2004 and entered new hedges in February 2006 (subsequent event). United also bears all fuel costs of its capacity-purchase United Express carriers.

UAL had fuel hedges outstanding at 12/31/2006: 32% of Q1 2007 and 4% of Q2 2007 forecasted consumption via crude oil collars, swaps and three-way collars. Net fair value of fuel derivatives was negative $2 million; mainline consumed 2,290 million gallons in 2006.

UAL Corp (United Air Lines) had fuel collar hedges outstanding at 12/31/2007 covering 13% of forecasted Q1 2008 and 13% of full-year 2008 consumption. Net fuel derivative fair value was $20 million; it consumed 2,292 million mainline gallons in 2007.

UAL had an active jet fuel hedging program at 12/31/2008 using calls, collars, 3-way and 4-way collars, plus purchased puts, covering 50% of Q1 2009 and 34% of full-year 2009 projected fuel. Fuel derivatives were a net payable of $867 million, and less than 1% of 2010 consumption was hedged.

UAL Corp's FY2009 10-K shows an active jet-fuel hedging program. At 12/31/2009 it had hedged about 36% of 2010 consolidated fuel consumption using swaps and purchased calls, and the fuel derivatives are not designated for hedge accounting.

Combined UAL/United/Continental FY2010 10-K. At Dec 31, 2010 Continental had 28% of 2011 expected fuel consumption hedged at the maximum-price level (18% at the minimum-price level) using WTI swaps, call options and collars. Its fuel hedge asset was $98M, and all hedges were designated as cash flow hedges.

Combined 10-K of United Continental Holdings, United Air Lines and Continental Airlines (FY2011). Fuel hedging is active; the 2012 coverage table is for UAL consolidated (31% max price / 23% min price), and Continental's own net fuel-derivative fair value is $29 million.

United Continental Holdings (FY2012 10-K) routinely hedges fuel and had about 31% of projected 2013 and 2% of projected 2014 fuel requirements hedged at year-end, using swaps, call options, collars and three-way collars. Net fuel derivative fair value was an asset of $46 million.

United Continental (UAL) had fuel hedges outstanding at 12/31/2013 covering about 24% of projected 2014 fuel (951 million gallons) and 8% of 2015 (309 million gallons). It used swaps, call options, collars, three-ways and four-way collars. Net fuel derivative fair value was an asset of $104 million.

United Continental (UAL and United Airlines, FY2014) had active fuel hedges at 12/31/2014: about 22% of projected 2015 fuel requirements (859 million gallons) and 1% of 2016 (35 million gallons). The net fuel hedge fair value was a liability of $717 million on one line and $(239) million on a net-of-collateral line.

United Continental Holdings had fuel hedges outstanding at 12/31/2015 covering about 17% of projected 2016 fuel requirements (652 million gallons). The fuel hedges had a net liability fair value of $124 million.

United Continental Holdings had no fuel hedging contracts outstanding at December 31, 2016, settled its last hedges in December 2016, and states its current strategy is not to hedge fuel. Fuel consumed in 2016 was 3,904 million gallons.

United Continental Holdings had no outstanding fuel hedges at 12/31/2017 and its current strategy is not to hedge fuel; the last designated fuel hedges expired in December 2016. It consumed 3,978 million gallons in 2017.

United Continental Holdings (FY2018 10-K) states it does not currently hedge fuel and has no open fuel derivatives. It settled all fuel hedges in 2016 and has not entered new ones. Fuel consumed in 2018 was 4,137 million gallons.

United Airlines Holdings' FY2019 10-K states the company does not currently hedge its future fuel requirements; its current strategy is not to enter into fuel hedge transactions. It consumed 4,292 million gallons in 2019, and regional carriers' fuel costs are borne by United under capacity purchase agreements.

United (UAL) FY2020 10-K states its current strategy is not to hedge fuel and that it does not currently hedge future fuel requirements. No fuel derivative positions are disclosed; regional CPA fuel costs are borne by United.

United Airlines Holdings FY2021 10-K states the company does not currently hedge future fuel requirements and its current strategy is not to enter into fuel hedge transactions. No fuel derivative positions are reported; 2,729 million gallons were consumed in 2021.

United Airlines Holdings FY2022 10-K states it does not currently hedge future fuel requirements and its strategy is not to enter hedging transactions. No fuel derivative positions are reported; fuel costs of regional partners under CPAs are borne by United.

United Airlines Holdings FY2023 10-K states it does not currently hedge future fuel requirements and its current strategy is not to enter fuel hedge transactions. No fuel derivative positions are disclosed; fuel costs of regional partners under CPAs are borne by United.

United Airlines Holdings states it does not currently hedge future fuel requirements and its strategy is not to enter into fuel hedge transactions. 2024 fuel consumption was 4,444 million gallons; regional CPA fuel costs are borne by United.

United Airlines Holdings states it does not currently hedge fuel price exposure and that its current strategy is not to enter into fuel hedging transactions. No fuel derivative positions are disclosed, and fuel under regional CPAs is borne by United.

America West (combined Holdings/AWA 10-K for FY2002) had costless collars on heating oil futures at 12/31/2002 covering about 40% of projected 2003 fuel, 63% of Q1 2003. Net fair value of the derivatives was a net asset of about $3.6 million; the program is designated as cash flow hedges.

Combined 10-K for America West Holdings and its subsidiary America West Airlines for FY2003. Costless collars on heating oil futures were outstanding at 12/31/2003 covering about 11% of projected 2004 fuel (39% of Q1 2004), with a net fair value asset of about $21.2 million.

America West had an active fuel hedging program at 12/31/2004: costless collars on heating oil futures and basis swaps covering about 42% of projected 2005 fuel requirements (67% Q1, 46% Q2, 36% Q3, 20% Q4). Net fair value was a net asset of about $0.2 million, and hedge accounting was disqualified in a February 2005 restatement.

FedEx Corp's FY ended May 31, 2002 10-K says it closed its jet fuel hedges in Q4 2001, entered no new fuel hedges in 2002 and had no derivative instruments outstanding at May 31, 2002. It relies on dynamic fuel surcharges instead.

FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2003) had no fuel derivatives outstanding. It closed its jet fuel hedges in 2001 and entered no new ones in 2002 or 2003. Dynamic fuel surcharges have taken the place of hedging.

FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2004) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because its dynamic fuel surcharge mitigates fuel price risk. No fuel positions, gallons or fair values are given in the excerpts.
FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2005) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because of its dynamic fuel surcharge. No fuel derivative positions, gallons hedged or fair values are disclosed.
FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2006) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because its indexed fuel surcharges recover fuel costs. No positions, gallons or fair values are disclosed.
FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2007) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because of its indexed fuel surcharges. Fuel price risk is described as largely mitigated by surcharges.

FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2008) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because its indexed fuel surcharges recover fuel costs. No fuel derivative positions, fair values or gallons are given in the excerpts.
FedEx Corporation's FY2009 10-K states that, because of its indexed fuel surcharge, it has no jet fuel hedging contracts. No positions, fair values or gallon figures are given in the excerpts.
FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2010) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because its indexed fuel surcharges recover fuel cost. No positions, gallons or fair values are given in the excerpts.
FedEx states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because its indexed fuel surcharge offsets fuel price changes. No fuel derivative positions are disclosed.

FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2012) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because its indexed fuel surcharges pass through fuel cost. No fuel derivative positions, gallons, or fair values are disclosed.
FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2013) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because of its indexed fuel surcharges. No positions, gallons or fuel derivative fair values are given in the excerpts.

FedEx Corporation's FY2014 (May 31, 2014) 10-K states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because of its indexed fuel surcharge. No fuel derivative positions, gallons or fair values are disclosed in the excerpts.
FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2015) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because of its indexed fuel surcharge. No positions, fair values or gallons are given in the excerpts.

FedEx Corporation's FY2016 (year ended May 31, 2016) 10-K says it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because of its indexed fuel surcharge. It reports no fuel derivative positions, and the only derivatives mentioned are TNT Express foreign-currency contracts.
FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2017) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts because of its indexed fuel surcharges. Its only derivatives disclosed are foreign-currency instruments at TNT Express.
FedEx states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts and no fuel derivatives at May 31, 2018, and no plans to use them, relying on indexed fuel surcharges. Its derivatives are foreign-currency only.
FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2019) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts and no fuel derivatives at year-end, relying on indexed fuel surcharges. Its only derivatives are foreign-currency ones.

FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2020) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts and no fuel derivative instruments at year-end; fuel price risk is mitigated by indexed fuel surcharges. No positions, gallons or fair values are reported in the excerpts.
FedEx's FY2021 10-K (year ended May 31, 2021) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts and no fuel derivatives at year-end. Fuel price risk is mitigated through indexed fuel surcharges.
FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2022) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts and no fuel derivative instruments at year-end; fuel price risk is mitigated by indexed fuel surcharges.

FedEx Corp's FY2023 10-K (year ended May 31, 2023) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts and no derivative financial instruments for fuel price exposure at year-end. Fuel price risk is mitigated through indexed fuel surcharges.
FedEx states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts and no fuel derivatives at May 31, 2024; fuel price risk is mitigated through indexed fuel surcharges. Its only derivatives are cross-currency swaps.
FedEx (FY ended May 31, 2025) states it has no jet fuel hedging contracts and no fuel derivatives at year-end, with no plans to use them. Fuel price risk is mitigated through indexed fuel surcharges.

Northwest Airlines Corp's FY1999 10-K reports active fuel hedging using exchange-traded futures and fuel swaps, with about 24% of 2000 fuel requirements hedged at December 31, 1999. Gallons consumed in 1999 were 2,039 million; the filing gives a $19 million unrealized gain in OCI on the hedges.

Northwest Airlines Corp FY2000 10-K: uses exchange-traded futures and fuel swaps; about 12% of Q1 2001 fuel requirements hedged at 12/31/2000. Fuel consumed was 2,113 million gallons in 2000. Net fair value is only described as a nominal unrealized gain.

Northwest Airlines (FY2002 10-K) had active fuel hedging at year-end: about 71% of Q1 2003 and 60% of full-year 2003 fuel requirements hedged using futures, swaps and options. Policy maximum hedge span is 18 months. Cash flow hedge accounting is used; $22 million of unrealized gains sit in OCI.

Northwest Airlines Corp's FY2003 10-K states it manages fuel price risk from time to time with futures, swaps and options, but had no fuel hedges in place at December 31, 2003 (versus 60% of 2003 full-year requirements hedged a year earlier). Fuel hedges reduced 2003 fuel costs by $105 million.

Northwest Airlines had fuel futures outstanding at 12/31/2004 covering approximately 25% of Q1 2005 and 6% of full-year 2005 mainline fuel requirements. Fuel gallons consumed in 2004 were 1,766 million. Hedges are designated as cash flow hedges.

Northwest Airlines (Chapter 11 debtor) had no fuel hedges in place at 12/31/2005 or through the filing date, though it states it hedges from time to time and has a policy of up to 18 months. Fuel hedges reduced 2005 fuel costs by $21 million (realized).

Northwest Airlines (Chapter 11 debtor-in-possession), FY2006. At 12/31/2006 it had hedged about 35% of projected 2007 fuel with crude oil collars (about 30%) and fixed-price swaps (about 10%); none were designated for hedge accounting.

Northwest Airlines had fuel collar options outstanding at 12/31/2007 covering about 10% of projected 2008 fuel requirements (18% including collars added in Jan/Feb 2008); all expire by 12/31/2008. The collars were not designated for hedge accounting.

Northwest Airlines Corp (FY2008 10-K) had fuel hedges outstanding at 12/31/2008 covering about 22% of projected 2009 fuel through crude/heating oil collars, three-way collars and swaps, all expiring by end of 2009. Hedge accounting is mixed, and 64% of Q1 2009 was hedged as of Jan 31, 2009.

UPS (a package carrier with an airline operation, not a passenger airline) uses options, swaps and futures on refined fuels covering up to one year. The net fair value was a $(5) million liability at 12/31/2000, accounted for as cash flow hedges. No coverage percentages or gallons are printed in the excerpts.

UPS (an integrated package carrier, not a pure passenger airline) uses options, swaps and futures on fuel and energy, designated as cash flow hedges, covering forecast consumption up to one year. The excerpts give no gallons or percent coverage, and the $34 million net fair value combines fuel and energy products.

UPS (FY2003 10-K) uses options, swaps and futures on refined fuels (jet-A, diesel, unleaded gasoline) and other energy products, covering forecasted consumption up to one year, designated as cash flow hedges. No gallons or coverage percentages are given, and the $30 million net fair value mixes fuel with natural gas and electricity.

UPS (a package carrier with an airline) uses options, swaps and futures to partly hedge jet-A, diesel, unleaded gasoline and also natural gas and electricity. The net fair value was an asset of $101 million at 12/31/2004. The excerpts give no percentage or gallons hedged.

UPS (a package carrier with an airline) uses options, swaps and futures on refined fuels and energy, designated as cash flow hedges, with a net asset of $192 million at 12/31/2005 that combines fuel and energy. No per-period coverage percentages or gallons are in the excerpts.

UPS (FY2006 10-K) uses options, swaps and futures on jet-A, diesel and unleaded gasoline (plus natural gas and electricity), designated as cash flow hedges, so the program is active. The excerpts give no coverage percentages, gallons, or fuel-only fair value; the combined fuel and energy net fair value was an asset of $10 million.

UPS (a package carrier with an airline, not a pure airline) uses options contracts for partial protection against fuel and energy price changes, with a net fair value of $(179) million at 12/31/2007, designated as cash flow hedges. The excerpts give no gallons or percent coverage by period.

UPS FY2008 10-K says it uses fuel surcharges as its primary fuel-risk tool plus options contracts for partial protection of fuel and energy prices, designated as cash flow hedges. Net fair value of these contracts was $0 at 12/31/2008 (versus $(179) million in 2007), and no coverage percentages or gallons are disclosed.

UPS (parcel carrier with an air network, not a passenger airline) says it periodically uses fuel option contracts but had none outstanding at 12/31/2009 and 2008. Fuel surcharges are its primary protection.

UPS (a package carrier, not a passenger airline) periodically uses fuel option contracts but had no commodity option contracts or commodity hedge positions outstanding at December 31, 2010 or 2009. Fuel surcharges are the primary means of managing fuel price risk.

UPS (a package and freight carrier, not a passenger airline) says it periodically uses fuel option contracts, but it had no commodity option contracts or hedge positions outstanding at December 31, 2011. Fuel surcharges are its primary protection against fuel price changes.

UPS (a parcel/package carrier with an air fleet, not a passenger airline) says it periodically uses fuel option contracts but had no commodity hedge positions outstanding at December 31, 2012. Fuel surcharges are its primary protection against fuel price changes.

UPS (a package and freight carrier, not a pure airline) says it periodically uses fuel option, forward and futures contracts but had no commodity hedge positions outstanding at 12/31/2013. It relies mainly on indexed fuel surcharges.

UPS (a package and logistics company, not a pure airline) periodically uses option, forward and futures contracts for fuel but had no commodity contracts outstanding at 12/31/2014 or 12/31/2013. Fuel surcharges are the primary means of reducing fuel price risk.

UPS (a package/logistics carrier with an airline, not a pure airline) states it periodically uses option, forward and futures contracts on fuel, but had no commodity contracts or hedge positions outstanding at Dec 31, 2015 and 2014. Fuel surcharges are the primary risk-mitigation tool.

UPS (a package carrier, not a passenger airline) states it periodically uses option, forward and futures contracts on fuel but had no commodity contracts or commodity hedge positions outstanding at December 31, 2016 and 2015. Fuel surcharges are the primary means of managing fuel price risk.

UPS (a package carrier, not a passenger airline) states it periodically uses option, forward and futures contracts on fuel, but had no commodity contracts or commodity hedge positions outstanding at December 31, 2017 and 2016. Fuel surcharges are its primary means of managing fuel price risk.

UPS (a package carrier, not a passenger airline) says it periodically enters into fuel derivatives but had no outstanding commodity hedge positions at December 31, 2018. Fuel surcharges are its primary means of reducing fuel price risk.

UPS (a package carrier, not an airline) states it periodically enters fuel derivative contracts but had no outstanding commodity hedge positions at 12/31/2019 and 2018. Fuel surcharges are its primary means of managing fuel price risk.

UPS (FY2020 10-K) states it had no outstanding commodity hedge positions at 12/31/2020 and 2019; fuel risk is mitigated primarily through indexed fuel surcharges, and hedging is used 'from time to time'. Only currency and interest-rate derivatives are outstanding.

UPS (FY2021 10-K) states it had no outstanding commodity hedge positions at 12/31/2021 and 2020. It relies mainly on fuel surcharges and mentions fuel hedging only 'from time to time'. Its derivatives in the excerpts are currency and interest-rate only.

UPS (a package and logistics carrier, not purely an airline) says fuel surcharges are its primary means of managing fuel price risk and that it may use hedging from time to time. It had no outstanding commodity hedge positions at 12/31/2022 or 12/31/2021.
UPS FY2023 10-K: no outstanding commodity hedge positions at year-end 2023 or 2022; fuel surcharges are the primary fuel-risk tool; only currency and interest-rate derivatives outstanding.

UPS (a package and freight carrier, not a conventional airline) states it had no outstanding commodity hedge positions at 12/31/2024 and 2023. It relies on fuel surcharges as the primary means of reducing fuel price risk.

UPS (a parcel and logistics carrier, not a conventional airline) reports no outstanding commodity hedge positions at 12/31/2025 and 12/31/2024. It relies on fuel surcharges as the primary means of managing fuel price risk.

JetBlue (FY2002 10-K) runs a crude oil option hedging program begun in 2001. At 12/31/2002 it had hedged about 45% of projected 2003 fuel and about 18% of projected 2004 fuel through Q1 2004. Derivatives were designated as cash flow hedges in December 2002.

JetBlue (FY2003 10-K) has an active fuel hedging program using crude oil options and swaps, with about 40% of projected 2004 fuel requirements hedged at year-end. Net derivative fair value was $10,992 thousand and the contracts are designated as cash flow hedges.

JetBlue (FY2004 10-K) has an active fuel hedging program using crude oil options and swaps; about 20% of projected 2005 fuel requirements were hedged at year-end (22% in the note and outlook), with net fair value of $20,487 thousand. All contracts are designated cash flow hedges and settle within 12 months.

JetBlue FY2005 10-K: active fuel hedging program using crude and heating oil options and swaps; about 30% of projected 2006 fuel requirements hedged at year-end, all settling by end of 2006. Net fair value of derivatives was $1 million, none designated as cash flow hedges.

JetBlue (FY2006 10-K) has an active fuel hedging program using crude and heating oil options and swaps, with about 38% of projected 2007 fuel requirements hedged at year-end 2006 and a net derivative liability of $15 million.

JetBlue (FY2007 10-K) runs an active fuel hedging program using crude and heating oil options and swaps, with about 13% of projected 2008 fuel requirements hedged at year-end 2007 and a net derivative asset of $33 million. All contracts settle by end of 2008, and 100% are designated as cash flow hedges.

JetBlue FY2008 10-K: crude/heating oil options and swaps; about 8% of projected 2009 fuel requirements hedged at year-end. The company then exited open swaps via reverse swaps and suspended its program in Q4 2008, so the economic position is effectively closed out while losses remain deferred in OCI.

JetBlue (FY2009 10-K) resumed fuel hedging in Q2 2009 after suspending it in Q4 2008, using crude call options, heating oil collars and jet fuel swaps. At 12/31/2009 it had about 40% of 2010 requirements hedged (the Item 1 text says 3% for 2011; MD&A says 6% for 1H 2011), with a net fuel derivative asset of $28 million.

JetBlue (FY2010 10-K) had active fuel hedges at 12/31/2010: about 28% of projected 2011 and 6% of projected 2012 fuel, using crude oil caps and collars, heating oil collars and jet fuel swaps. Net fuel derivative fair value was a $23 million asset, and all outstanding contracts were designated cash flow hedges.

JetBlue (FY2011 10-K) had active fuel hedges at 12/31/2011: swaps, collars and crude caps covering about 27% of projected 2012 fuel, with quarterly coverage of 35%/20%/15%/15% for designated contracts. Net fuel derivative fair value was a $4 million liability; 525 million gallons were consumed in 2011.

JetBlue (FY2012 10-K) had Brent crude collars outstanding at 12/31/2012 covering 8%, 8% and 4% of Q1-Q3 2013 projected fuel (about 5% of full-year 2013), plus 6% of 2013 under fixed forward price agreements. Net fuel derivative fair value was a $1 million liability.

JetBlue had outstanding fuel hedges at 12/31/2013 (jet fuel swaps and caps) covering about 9% of 2014 consumption, plus 7% under fixed forward price agreements. Net fuel derivative fair value was a $6 million asset.

JetBlue (FY2014 10-K) had active fuel hedges at year-end 2014: swaps and collars on jet fuel and heating oil, covering 14-20% of projected 2015 fuel use by quarter (about 17% overall in Item 7A). Net fuel derivative liability was $51 million after collateral; it consumed 639 million gallons in 2014.

JetBlue had fuel swaps outstanding at 12/31/2015 covering about 10% of projected Q3 and Q4 2016 fuel usage (about 5% of 2016 requirements overall), with a net $5 million liability. Its hedges are designated cash flow hedges.

JetBlue FY2016 10-K: active fuel hedging with swaps, caps, collars on jet fuel, crude and heating oil. About 10% of projected 2017 fuel hedged at year-end (10% in each 2017 quarter, all jet fuel swaps), 1,920 thousand barrels hedged volume, net fair value asset of $22 million.

JetBlue (FY2017 10-K) describes an ongoing discretionary fuel hedging approach (swaps, caps, collars, basis swaps) but had no fuel hedge contracts outstanding at December 31, 2017. It recorded $15 million of hedge gains in 2017 and 792 million gallons consumed.

JetBlue (FY2018 10-K) had jet fuel call option hedges outstanding at 12/31/2018 covering about 4% of projected 2019 fuel, 7% in each of Q1 and Q2 2019, all settling by June 30, 2019. Fair value was immaterial, and the company designates these as cash flow hedges.

JetBlue (FY2019 10-K) had outstanding jet fuel call option spreads at 12/31/2019 covering 20% of Q1 2020 and 19% of Q2 2020 fuel, about 10% of projected 2020 requirements, all settling by June 30, 2020. Net fuel derivative asset was $8 million, designated as cash flow hedges.

JetBlue describes an ongoing discretionary fuel hedging approach but had no fuel hedges outstanding at 12/31/2020. Hedged volume and fair value were nil at year-end 2020, versus 2,112 thousand barrels and an $8 million asset at 2019 year-end.

JetBlue describes an ongoing discretionary fuel hedging approach (options, swaps, collars on jet fuel, crude and heating oil) but had no fuel hedges outstanding at December 31, 2021 or 2020. Realized hedge losses were $7 million in 2020 and none in 2021.

JetBlue (FY2022 10-K) had call option spread fuel hedges outstanding at 12/31/2022 covering 8.8% of Q1 2023 projected fuel usage, with a $3 million asset fair value; it hedged more Q2/Q3 2023 in February 2023 (subsequent event).

JetBlue had outstanding jet fuel call option spreads at 12/31/2023 covering 30% of Q1 2024, 16% Q2, 3% Q3 and 5% Q4 projected fuel usage, designated as cash flow hedges. Asset fair value was $4 million; 897 million gallons were consumed in 2023.

JetBlue (FY2024) describes a discretionary fuel hedging approach (call spread options on jet fuel used in 2024) but had no outstanding fuel hedging contracts at December 31, 2024. Fuel consumption was 853 million gallons in 2024.

JetBlue FY2025 10-K states it periodically hedges fuel on a discretionary basis (call spreads in 2024 and 2023) but had no outstanding fuel hedging contracts at December 31, 2025 or 2024. Percentage of consumption hedged was 0 in 2025 versus 24% in 2024 and 25% in 2023.

Republic Airways (FY2004 10-K) is a regional carrier whose fuel cost is passed through or trued-up by its code-share partners. It entered no fuel swaps in 2003 or 2004, and the excerpts show no fuel derivative positions outstanding at year-end 2004. The only 2002 fuel swaps were not designated as hedges.

Republic Airways (FY2005) operates 100% fixed-fee code-share flying with fuel reimbursed by partners. The excerpts show no fuel derivative positions at year-end and no explicit statement about a hedging program; fuel swaps are mentioned only in the past tense.

Republic Airways (FY2006 10-K) is a fixed-fee regional carrier whose partners pay for or reimburse fuel. The excerpts have no statement on fuel derivatives or fuel hedging, so program status is not_discussed. The only hedges described are interest-rate treasury locks.

Republic Airways FY2007 10-K excerpts contain no statement on fuel hedging or fuel derivatives; the only derivatives described are settled treasury locks (interest rate). Fuel is a pass-through cost to partners, and several partners buy fuel directly.

Republic Airways is a regional carrier under fixed-fee code-share agreements. Fuel is supplied directly by partners or passed through, and the excerpts show no fuel derivatives. Its only derivatives are interest-rate swaps.

Republic Airways (FY2009 10-K) holds purchased Gulf Coast Jet A call options outstanding at year-end covering Q2 and Q3 2010 (14.3% each); not designated as hedges. Fuel is largely pass-through for the fixed-fee business, but the branded Midwest/Frontier operations buy their own fuel.

Republic Airways (FY2010) periodically uses call options, swaps and collars on crude oil derivatives, undesignated; Frontier operation had 5% of anticipated volume hedged for Q2-Q4 2011 at year-end. Fixed-fee partner fuel is pass-through or supplied directly by partners.

Republic Airways periodically buys call options, swaps or collars on oil derivatives for its branded (Frontier) operations, but had no hedge position or fuel derivatives at 12/31/2011. Fixed-fee partners supply or reimburse fuel.

Republic Airways (owner of Frontier) periodically buys call options, swaps and collars on crude oil derivatives, not designated as hedges. At 12/31/2012 it had a hedge on 15% of anticipated fuel volume through Q2 2013, with an immaterial fair value. Fixed-fee partners supply or reimburse fuel.
Republic Airways' FY2013 10-K excerpts contain no statement about fuel hedging. All code-share partners supply fuel directly, and Item 7A mentions fuel price risk only 'to a limited extent'.

Republic Airways (FY2014 10-K) is a regional carrier whose code-share partners supply all fuel, so it has no meaningful fuel exposure. The excerpts describe no fuel derivatives or fixed-price fuel commitments outstanding at year-end.

Republic Airways (FY2015 10-K) is a capacity-purchase regional carrier whose partners (American, Delta, United) supply all fuel; the excerpts contain no statement about fuel hedging, derivatives positions or a hedging program.

Hawaiian Holdings (FY2002) uses heating oil forward contracts to hedge up to 50% of anticipated fuel needs, with $7.4 million of contracts outstanding at year-end through April 2003, plus a fixed-price jet fuel purchase agreement for 2003. No coverage percentage or gallons are stated for the outstanding positions.

Hawaiian Holdings' FY2003 10-K (Hawaiian Airlines in Chapter 11, deconsolidated from April 2003) states Hawaiian held heating oil forward contracts with a $1.6 million notional through March 2004 at year-end, under a strategy of hedging up to 50% of anticipated fuel needs. No gallons, percentage coverage, or fair value are given.

Hawaiian Holdings' subsidiary Hawaiian Airlines resumed heating oil hedging in September 2004. At December 31, 2004 it held forward contracts with a $14.9 million notional through May 2005, designated as cash flow hedges. As of March 18, 2005 it held about 33.8 million gallons of heating oil, a subsequent event.

Hawaiian Holdings (FY2005) had jet fuel forward contracts outstanding at 12/31/2005 with fair value of $2.4 million, covering approximately 30% of anticipated 2006 fuel needs. Fuel consumed in 2005 was 111,220 thousand gallons, and the hedges were designated as cash flow hedges from September 1, 2005.

Hawaiian Holdings (FY2006 10-K) has an active jet fuel forward hedging program. At 12/31/2006 it had hedged about 28%, 9% and 1% of Q1-Q3 2007 fuel; the net obligation was $1.1 million. Hedges are designated as cash flow hedges.

Hawaiian Holdings had an active fuel hedging program at 12/31/2007, mainly NYMEX heating oil futures plus a small amount of jet fuel forwards. It had hedged about 25%, 8% and 1% of Q1, Q2 and Q3 2008 fuel needs.

Hawaiian Holdings' FY2008 10-K reports an active fuel hedging program using crude oil and heating oil call options, collars, futures and swaps. About 49%, 29% and 9% of Q1 to Q3 2009 fuel needs were hedged at year-end, and the net fuel derivative liability was $10.0 million. Most derivatives were not designated for hedge accounting.

Hawaiian Holdings had an active fuel hedging program at 12/31/2009 using crude oil call options and collars, plus heating oil futures/swaps, covering 36 million gallons over the next twelve months. Derivatives were not designated for hedge accounting, with a net fair value asset of $3.6 million.

Hawaiian Holdings had fuel derivatives (crude oil caps and collars) outstanding at 12/31/2010 covering 49.9 million gallons, with a net fair value asset of $8.8 million, not designated for hedge accounting. The Q1 2011 to Q1 2012 coverage table is dated January 26, 2011, not year-end.
